title: What are SLI, SLO, and SLA, and how do they relate (indicator → internal objective → external contract)?
shortTitle: SLI, SLO, and SLA and how they relate (indicator, internal objective, external contract)
topicTitle: What are SLI, SLO, and SLA, and how do they relate

s1_definition.profdef: An SLI, a Service Level Indicator, is a precisely measured quantity describing some aspect of service behaviour, such as the proportion of requests served successfully or the proportion served under a latency threshold. An SLO, a Service Level Objective, is an internal target for an SLI over a time window, for example 99.95 percent success over 28 days. An SLA, a Service Level Agreement, is an external contract with customers that promises a level of service and specifies consequences, such as financial credits, when it is not met. The relationship is a progression: the indicator is what you measure, the objective is the internal goal you hold yourself to, and the agreement is the external promise, which is deliberately set looser than the objective so you have internal buffer.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, the SLI is the actual measured number — "out of every thousand transfers Rajesh and Priya attempt, how many succeed." The SLO is the bank's internal promise to itself — "we will keep that at 99.95 percent or better this month, and if it slips we stop shipping risky changes." The SLA is the written contract the bank signs with a corporate client — "we guarantee 99.9 percent, and if we fall below it we refund part of your fee." Notice the internal goal of 99.95 is stricter than the contract of 99.9; that gap is the safety cushion so a bad week does not instantly breach a legal contract.
s1_definition.oneliner: SLI is what you measure, SLO is the internal target you hold yourself to, and SLA is the external contract with penalties — and you set the SLO stricter than the SLA to keep a buffer.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An SLI, a Service Level Indicator, is a precisely measured quantity describing some aspect of service behaviour, such as the proportion of requests served successfully or the proportion served under a latency threshold. An SLO, a Service Level Objective, is an internal target for an SLI over a time window, for example 99.95 percent success over 28 days. An SLA, a Service Level Agreement, is an external contract with customers that promises a level of service and specifies consequences, such as financial credits, when it is not met. The relationship is a progression: the indicator is what you measure, the objective is the internal goal you hold yourself to, and the agreement is the external promise, which is deliberately set looser than the objective so you have internal buffer.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, the SLI is the actual measured number — "out of every thousand transfers Rajesh and Priya attempt, how many succeed." The SLO is the bank's internal promise to itself — "we will keep that at 99.95 percent or better this month, and if it slips we stop shipping risky changes." The SLA is the written contract the bank signs with a corporate client — "we guarantee 99.9 percent, and if we fall below it we refund part of your fee." Notice the internal goal of 99.95 is stricter than the contract of 99.9; that gap is the safety cushion so a bad week does not instantly breach a legal contract.

**One line to remember:** SLI is what you measure, SLO is the internal target you hold yourself to, and SLA is the external contract with penalties — and you set the SLO stricter than the SLA to keep a buffer.

sections.s2_technical:
An SLI must be a well-defined ratio of good events to total valid events, expressed as a percentage, because that form is easy to reason about and to set a target on. A good availability SLI is "the number of successful HTTP responses divided by the number of valid HTTP requests." A good latency SLI is "the number of requests served faster than 300 milliseconds divided by the total number of requests." You define it carefully: which responses count as good (usually 2xx and some 4xx that are the client's fault), what counts as a valid request, and where you measure it (ideally from the load balancer or client, close to the user). A badly defined SLI, like raw average latency, hides problems, which is why percentiles and ratios are preferred.

An SLO is a target on that SLI over a rolling window. For example, "99.9 percent of valid requests succeed over a rolling 28-day window." The window matters: too short and normal variance trips it constantly, too long and a sustained problem hides. The SLO is the single most important reliability number for a team because everything else flows from it — the error budget, the alerting, and the decision of whether to prioritise new features or reliability work. You pick the SLO based on what users actually need, not an aspirational "100 percent," because 100 percent is impossibly expensive and users cannot even perceive the difference between 99.9 and 100 percent given their own network and devices.

An SLA is a contract, usually written by the business and legal teams, that promises a level to paying customers and attaches consequences. If the bank promises 99.9 percent monthly availability and delivers only 99.5 percent, the SLA might require service credits refunded to the customer. Because an SLA has legal and financial teeth, you never set it equal to your internal SLO. You set the SLA looser — say the SLA is 99.9 but the SLO is 99.95 — so that your team gets an internal alarm and a chance to react well before you are anywhere near breaching the customer contract. Many internal services have SLOs but no SLA at all, because there is no external customer to sign a contract with.

The relationship is a clean progression. The SLI is the measurement. The SLO is the internal objective set on that measurement, stricter and used to drive engineering decisions. The SLA is the external, contractual promise, looser than the SLO, with defined penalties. A senior nuance: you should have only a handful of SLOs per service covering what users truly care about — typically availability and latency, sometimes correctness or freshness — because too many SLOs dilute focus, and each SLO should be owned, reviewed, and reported. The SLO is also what you alert on via error-budget burn, which is the subject of a closely related concept.
sections.s3_banking:
The National Bank of India's transfer service needs reliability targets. The team must define an SLI, set an internal SLO, and sign an external SLA with a corporate client, then continuously measure whether reality meets each.

Problem 1 — The team measures the SLI: out of the transfers Rajesh, Priya, and other customers attempt, what fraction succeed. This is the raw indicator computed from counts of good and total events.

Problem 2 — The team sets an internal SLO of 99.95 percent and an external SLA of 99.9 percent, deliberately keeping the SLA looser so there is a buffer.

Problem 3 — As traffic flows, the system must report the current SLI and classify the situation: meeting the SLO (all good), below the SLO but above the SLA (internal alarm, react now, but no contract breach), or below the SLA (contract breach with penalties).

Our runnable Java simulation models an `SliCalculator` that computes the success ratio from good and total counts, and a `ServiceLevels` holder with the SLO and SLA targets whose `classify()` returns the status. Classes: `SliCalculator`, `ServiceLevels`, and an `SloDemo` main that feeds healthy, degraded, and breaching traffic.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a transfer service with an internal SLO of 99.95 percent and an external SLA of 99.9 percent, measured across three traffic phases.

Step 1: The system records the healthy phase — out of ten thousand transfers, only two failed. The SLI calculator divides good events by total and produces 99.98 percent. Because this is at or above the SLO, the service is classified as meeting the SLO and everything is healthy.

Step 2: The system records a degraded phase where eight transfers failed out of ten thousand, giving an SLI of 99.92 percent. This is below the internal SLO of 99.95 but still above the external SLA of 99.9. The classification is "below SLO, above SLA" — an internal alarm that tells the team to react now, but critically there is no contract breach because the buffer between the SLO and the SLA absorbed the problem.

Step 3: The system records a breaching phase where twenty transfers failed out of ten thousand, giving an SLI of 99.80 percent. This is below even the external SLA, so the classification is SLA breach, which triggers contractual penalties such as service credits to the corporate client.

Step 4: Across the three phases, the progression is clear: the SLI is the measured number, the SLO is the stricter internal line that alarmed first, and the SLA is the looser external line whose breach has financial consequences.

```
2026-10-30 02:25:10 [INFO   ] National Bank of India — transfer service level targets
2026-10-30 02:25:10 [INFO   ] MEETING SLO: SLI 99.980% >= SLO 99.950% — healthy
2026-10-30 02:25:10 [WARNING] BELOW SLO (99.920% < 99.950%) but ABOVE SLA 99.900% — internal alarm, react now, NO contract breach (buffer working)
2026-10-30 02:25:10 [SEVERE ] SLA BREACH: SLI 99.800% < SLA 99.900% — contractual penalties (service credits)
```


sections.s6_takeaway:
An SLI, a Service Level Indicator, is a precisely measured quantity describing how the service behaves, expressed as a ratio of good events to total valid events — for example the fraction of transfers that succeed, or the fraction served faster than three hundred milliseconds. I always define it carefully: which responses count as good, what counts as a valid request, and where it is measured, ideally close to the user at the load balancer. An SLO, a Service Level Objective, is an internal target set on that indicator over a rolling window, such as 99.95 percent success over 28 days. The SLO is the most important reliability number a team owns, because the error budget, the alerting, and the decision between shipping features and doing reliability work all flow from it.

An SLA, a Service Level Agreement, is an external contract with paying customers that promises a level of service and attaches consequences, like service credits, when the promise is broken. Because an SLA has legal and financial teeth, I never set it equal to the internal SLO — I set the SLA looser than the SLO so the team gets an internal alarm and time to react well before the customer contract is anywhere near breached. Many internal services have SLOs but no SLA at all, simply because there is no external customer to sign a contract with.

The relationship is a clean progression from indicator to internal objective to external contract. In my project at the National Bank of India, the transfer service measured its SLI as the fraction of successful transfers for customers like Rajesh and Priya. We held an internal SLO of 99.95 percent and signed an external SLA of 99.9 percent with a corporate client. When a degradation pushed us to 99.92 percent, we were below our internal objective and the team was alarmed and reacting, but we were still above the contractual SLA, so there was no breach and no penalty — the deliberate buffer between the SLO and the SLA absorbed the problem exactly as designed. Only if we dropped below 99.9 percent would the SLA breach trigger service credits. The principle I always state is that you measure with SLIs, you hold yourself to a stricter internal SLO, and you promise customers a looser SLA, and the gap between the SLO and the SLA is the safety cushion that keeps a bad week from becoming a broken contract.
